statement: Let $v(x, t)$ be a $C^1$ [vector field](c:vector-field) on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with [flow map](c:flow-map) $\varphi_t$, let $\Omega_0$ be a bounded open set, $\Omega(t) = \varphi_t(\Omega_0)$, and let $f(x, t)$ be $C^1$. Then $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega(t)} f\,dV = \int_{\Omega(t)} \big(\partial_t f + \nabla\cdot(f v)\big)\,dV$, which equals $\int_{\Omega(t)} \partial_t f\,dV + \int_{\partial\Omega(t)} f\,v\cdot n\,dA$ when $\partial\Omega(t)$ is smooth.

hypotheses.text: The velocity $v$ is a $C^1$ [vector field](c:vector-field) whose flow $\varphi_t$ is defined on $\overline{\Omega_0}$ for $t$ in an open interval.
The set $\Omega_0$ is open and bounded, so its closure is compact.
The function $f(x, t)$ is $C^1$ in $x$ and $t$.

conclusion: $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega(t)} f\,dV = \int_{\Omega(t)} \big(\partial_t f + \nabla\cdot(f v)\big)\,dV = \int_{\Omega(t)} \partial_t f\,dV + \int_{\partial\Omega(t)} f\,v\cdot n\,dA$, the last form for a smooth boundary.

proofs.name: Pull back to the initial region
proofs.slogan: Pull the integral back to the fixed region $\Omega_0$ by the flow, differentiate under the integral sign, and use $\partial_t J = (\nabla\cdot v)\,J$ for the Jacobian.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $t$ in the interval of the flow. The boundary form needs a smooth boundary $\partial\Omega(t)$ for the divergence theorem.

roles.why: The flow carries $\Omega_0$ to $\Omega(t)$, has $\partial_t\varphi_t = v(\varphi_t, t)$ and a positive Jacobian.
A compact closure makes the integrand and its time derivative uniformly bounded, so the derivative passes under the integral.
A $C^1$ integrand has the chain rule and a continuous time derivative.

steps.slogan: Pull the integral back to $\Omega_0$ by the substitution $x = \varphi_t(X)$.
steps.detail: The change of variables formula gives $\int_{\Omega(t)} f(x, t)\,dx = \int_{\Omega_0} f(\varphi_t(X), t)\,J(X, t)\,dX$ with $J = \det D\varphi_t$. Here $J > 0$, because $J(X, 0) = 1$ and $J$ is continuous and never zero.

steps.slogan: Differentiate under the integral sign over the fixed compact closure.
steps.detail: The integrand $f(\varphi_t(X), t)\,J(X, t)$ has a continuous $t$-derivative on the compact set $\overline{\Omega_0}$ times a small time interval. So $\frac{d}{dt}$ passes inside the integral over the fixed region $\Omega_0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the time derivative of $f(\varphi_t(X), t)$ by the chain rule.
steps.detail: Because $\partial_t \varphi_t(X) = v(\varphi_t(X), t)$, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt} f(\varphi_t(X), t) = \partial_t f + v\cdot\nabla f$, evaluated at $(\varphi_t(X), t)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant) satisfies $\partial_t J = (\nabla\cdot v)\,J$.
steps.detail: The matrix $A = D\varphi_t(X)$ solves $\partial_t A = Dv(\varphi_t(X), t)\,A$. Jacobi's formula gives $\partial_t \det A = \det A\,\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}\partial_t A) = J\,\operatorname{tr} Dv = J\,\nabla\cdot v$, the [divergence](c:divergence) of $v$.

steps.slogan: Combine the terms and push the integral forward to $\Omega(t)$.
steps.detail:
Steps 3 and 4 give the derivative of the integrand as $(\partial_t f + v\cdot
abla f + f\,
abla\cdot v)\,J = (\partial_t f + 
abla\cdot(f v))\,J$. The substitution of step 1, read backwards, gives $\int_{\Omega(t)} (\partial_t f + 
abla\cdot(f v))\,dV$.

steps.slogan: Turn the divergence term into a boundary flux by the divergence theorem.
steps.detail: For a smooth boundary with outer normal $n$, the divergence theorem gives $\int_{\Omega(t)} \nabla\cdot(f v)\,dV = \int_{\partial\Omega(t)} f\,v\cdot n\,dA$. This gives the second form of the formula.

concepts.c:vector-field: The velocity field moves the region and appears in the flux term.
concepts.c:flow-map: The flow map carries the fixed region to the moving region.
concepts.c:jacobian-determinant: The Jacobian determinant is the volume factor of the substitution.
concepts.c:divergence: The divergence of $v$ is the rate of change of the volume factor.

source.note: The standard proof by the flow substitution and the Jacobian identity, as in Chorin and Marsden, A Mathematical Introduction to Fluid Mechanics, section 1.1 (transport theorem).

statement: Let $V$ be a [normed space](c:normed-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If some closed [ball](c:ball) $\overline{B}(c, r)$ with $r > 0$ is [compact](c:compact-space), then $V$ is a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space).

hypotheses.text: The space $V$ is a [normed space](c:normed-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The radius $r$ is positive.
The closed ball $\overline{B}(c, r)$ is [compact](c:compact-space).

formal.difference: The declaration works over any complete nontrivially normed field and needs only a continuous scalar multiplication on the normed group $V$.

proofs.name: Finite net and rescaling
proofs.slogan: Cover the ball by finitely many half-size copies, iterate the cover, and trap the ball inside the span of the finitely many centres.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $V = 0$ there is nothing to prove.

roles.why: Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ makes finite-dimensional subspaces closed, and the norm makes the rescaled balls shrink.
A positive radius makes $U$ a neighborhood of $0$, so every vector rescales into $U$.
Compactness makes the ball [totally bounded](c:totally-bounded-space), which gives the finite net.

steps.slogan: Translate the compact ball to the ball $U = \overline{B}(0, r)$ around the origin.
steps.detail: The map $x \mapsto x - c$ is an isometry of $V$, so $U = \overline{B}(c, r) - c$ is compact. A compact metric space is [totally bounded](c:totally-bounded-space).

steps.slogan: Cover $U$ by finitely many translates $f + \tfrac12 U$ and span their centres.
steps.detail: Total boundedness gives a finite set $F$ with $U \subseteq F + \tfrac12 U$. The span $M$ of $F$ is a finite-dimensional [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace); it is complete, hence closed in $V$.

steps.slogan: Iterate the cover to get $U \subseteq M + 2^{-n} U$ for every $n$.
steps.detail: The case $n = 0$ holds with $0 \in M$. If $U \subseteq M + 2^{-n}U$, then $U \subseteq M + 2^{-n}(M + \tfrac12 U) = M + 2^{-n-1}U$, because $M$ is a subspace.

steps.slogan: Approximate each point of $U$ by points of the closed subspace $M$.
steps.detail: For $x \in U$ write $x = m_n + u_n$ with $m_n \in M$ and $\|u_n\| \le 2^{-n} r$. Then $m_n \to x$, and $M$ is closed, so $x \in M$. Hence $U \subseteq M$.

steps.slogan: Rescale every vector into $U$ to show that $M = V$.
steps.detail: For $v \ne 0$ the vector $(r/\|v\|)\,v$ lies in $U \subseteq M$, so $v \in M$. Hence $V = M$, which has finite dimension.

concepts.c:normed-space: The norm measures how fast the rescaled balls shrink.
concepts.c:ball: The compact closed ball is covered by its half-size copies.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the ball supplies the finite net.
concepts.c:finite-dimensional-vector-space: The span of the finite net is the whole space.
concepts.c:totally-bounded-space: Total boundedness gives finitely many half-size balls that cover.
concepts.c:linear-subspace: The span $M$ is a closed subspace that absorbs the cover.

proofs.name: Riesz's lemma and separated sequences
proofs.slogan: In an infinite-dimensional space, Riesz's lemma builds unit vectors that stay $1/2$ apart, so the compact ball has a sequence without convergent subsequence.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by contradiction: assume $V$ is infinite-dimensional.

roles.why: Finite-dimensional subspaces of a normed space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ are closed, so Riesz's lemma applies to them.
A positive radius keeps the scaled points $r/2$ apart.
A [compact](c:compact-space) metric space is sequentially compact.

steps.slogan: Find a unit vector at distance at least $1/2$ from a closed proper subspace.
steps.detail: Let $M$ be a closed proper subspace and $x \notin M$, so $d = \operatorname{dist}(x, M) > 0$. Pick $m \in M$ with $\|x - m\| \le 2d$. Then $y = (x - m)/\|x - m\|$ has $\operatorname{dist}(y, M) = d/\|x - m\| \ge 1/2$.

steps.slogan: Build unit vectors $y_1, y_2, \dots$ whose mutual distances are at least $1/2$.
steps.detail: Given $y_1, \dots, y_k$, their span $M_k$ is finite-dimensional, hence closed, and proper because $V$ is infinite-dimensional. Step 1 gives a unit $y_{k+1}$ with $\|y_{k+1} - y_j\| \ge 1/2$ for all $j \le k$.

steps.slogan: Move the sequence into the compact ball by $x_k = c + r\,y_k$.
steps.detail: Each $x_k$ lies in $\overline{B}(c, r)$, and $\|x_k - x_j\| = r\,\|y_k - y_j\| \ge r/2 > 0$ for $k \ne j$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the existence of a convergent subsequence in the compact ball.
steps.detail: The compact metric ball is sequentially compact, so some subsequence of $(x_k)$ converges and is Cauchy. Its terms stay $r/2$ apart, a contradiction. So $V$ is a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space).

concepts.c:normed-space: The norm gives the distances that Riesz's lemma controls.
concepts.c:ball: The separated sequence lives inside the compact closed ball.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness forces a convergent subsequence, which cannot exist.
concepts.c:finite-dimensional-vector-space: Finite-dimensional subspaces are closed and proper in an infinite-dimensional space.

source.note: The classical proof by Riesz's lemma (F. Riesz, 1918), as in Kreyszig, Introductory Functional Analysis with Applications, section 2.5.

statement: Let $p(s) = a_0 s^n + a_1 s^{n-1} + \dots + a_n$ be a real [polynomial](c:polynomial) with $n \ge 1$ and $a_0 > 0$. Let $\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_n$ be the leading principal minors of its [Hurwitz matrix](c:hurwitz-matrix) $(a_{2j-i})_{i,j=1}^{n}$, with $a_k = 0$ for $k < 0$ or $k > n$. Then every [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of $p$ has negative [real part](c:real-part) if and only if $\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_n > 0$.

hypotheses.text: The coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_n$ are real numbers.
The degree is $n \ge 1$ and the leading coefficient is $a_0 > 0$.

conclusion: All roots of $p$ lie in the open left half-plane exactly when all Hurwitz minors $\Delta_k$ are positive.

proofs.name: Routh step and continuity of roots
proofs.slogan: Lower the degree by one Routh step, show by root continuity that the step keeps stability, and match it with a row reduction of the Hurwitz matrix.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by induction on $n$. The case $a_1 \le 0$ is settled first, because then both sides of the equivalence fail.

roles.why: Real coefficients make the two alternate parts of $p$ real and imaginary on the imaginary axis.
The sign $a_0 > 0$ fixes the sign of $a_1$ for a stable $p$ and sends the escaping root to $-\infty$.

steps.slogan: Show that a [Hurwitz polynomial](c:hurwitz-polynomial) has $a_1 > 0$, and note $\Delta_1 = a_1$.
steps.detail: The roots sum to $-a_1/a_0$. If all have negative real part, the sum has negative real part, so $a_1 > 0$. Hence for $a_1 \le 0$ both sides fail, and the proof assumes $a_1 > 0$.

steps.slogan: Define the reduced polynomial $q = p - \eta\,s\,r$ with $\eta = a_0/a_1$.
steps.detail: Let $r(s) = a_1 s^{n-1} + a_3 s^{n-3} + \cdots$. Then $q(s) = a_1 s^{n-1} + (a_2 - \eta a_3)s^{n-2} + a_3 s^{n-3} + (a_4 - \eta a_5)s^{n-4} + \cdots$ has degree $n - 1$ and leading coefficient $a_1$.

steps.slogan: Deform $p$ into $q$ through $p_t = p - t\eta\,s\,r$ with fixed roots on the imaginary axis.
steps.detail: At $s = i\omega$, $r(i\omega)$ and the rest of $p_t(i\omega)$ lie on perpendicular lines, and only the rest depends on $t$. So $p_t(i\omega) = 0$ exactly when $p(i\omega) = 0$. As $t \to 1$, one root of $p_t$ escapes like $-a_1/((1 - t)a_0) \to -\infty$ and, by Hurwitz's theorem, the others tend to the roots of $q$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $p$ is Hurwitz if and only if $q$ is Hurwitz.
steps.detail: By step 3, $p$ and $q$ have the same roots on the imaginary axis, so if either is Hurwitz, no root of $p_t$ crosses the axis for $t \in [0, 1)$. The number of roots in the open left half-plane then stays constant, and comparing $t = 0$ with $t$ near $1$, where the escaping root is negative, gives the equivalence (Meinsma's lemma).

steps.slogan: Row-reduce the Hurwitz matrix to get $\Delta_k(p) = a_1\,\Delta_{k-1}(q)$ for $k \ge 2$.
steps.detail: Subtract $\eta$ times row $2m - 1$ from row $2m$ for each $m$. The first column becomes $(a_1, 0, \dots, 0)$ and the lower right block becomes the Hurwitz matrix of $q$; these row operations keep every leading principal minor, a [determinant](c:determinant).

steps.slogan: Induct on the degree to match the minors with the stability property.
steps.detail: For $n = 1$ the root $-a_1/a_0$ is negative exactly when $\Delta_1 = a_1 > 0$. For $n \ge 2$, all $\Delta_k(p) > 0$ if and only if $a_1 > 0$ and all $\Delta_j(q) > 0$, which by induction and step 4 means that $p$ is Hurwitz.

concepts.c:polynomial: The criterion reads stability off the polynomial's coefficients.
concepts.c:hurwitz-matrix: The minors of the Hurwitz matrix encode the repeated Routh steps.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: The roots move continuously while the polynomial is deformed.
concepts.c:real-part: Stability asks for roots with negative real part.
concepts.c:hurwitz-polynomial: A Hurwitz polynomial is the stable case the criterion detects.
concepts.c:determinant: Row operations keep the leading minors, which factor as $a_1\Delta_{k-1}(q)$.

source.note: Meinsma's continuity proof of the Routh step (G. Meinsma, Elementary proof of the Routh-Hurwitz test, Systems & Control Letters 25, 1995), with the classical row reduction from the Routh array to the Hurwitz minors.

statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be [finite](c:finite-set) subsets of a [group](c:group) $G$, written additively, with $B$ nonempty, and let the [sumset](c:sumset) satisfy $|A + B| \le K|B|$ for a real $K$. Then some $F \subseteq A$ with $|F| \le K$ satisfies $A \subseteq F + (B - B)$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $A$ and $B$ are [finite](c:finite-set).
The set $B$ is nonempty.
The [sumset](c:sumset) satisfies $|A + B| \le K|B|$.

conclusion: Some $F \subseteq A$ with $|F| \le K$ has $A \subseteq F + (B - B)$: at most $K$ translates of $B - B$ cover $A$.

proofs.name: Maximal disjoint translates
proofs.slogan: Take a maximal family of disjoint translates $a + B$ with $a \in A$; counting bounds its size and maximality gives the cover.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, in any group, commutative or not. For $A = \emptyset$ the set $F = \emptyset$ works.

roles.why: Finiteness gives a maximal family and finite cardinalities to compare.
A nonempty $B$ allows division by $|B|$ and puts $0$ in $B - B$.
The bound on $|A + B|$ bounds the number of disjoint translates.

steps.slogan: Choose a maximal $F \subseteq A$ whose translates $f + B$ are pairwise disjoint.
steps.detail: The subsets of $A$ with pairwise disjoint translates form a nonempty family, because $\emptyset$ belongs to it. The family is finite, so it has a [maximal element](c:maximal-element) $F$.

steps.slogan: Count the disjoint translates inside $A + B$ to get $|F| \le K$.
steps.detail: The sets $f + B$ for $f \in F$ are disjoint, each has $|B|$ elements, and all lie in $A + B$. So $|F|\,|B| \le |A + B| \le K|B|$, and $|B| > 0$ gives $|F| \le K$.

steps.slogan: Show that each translate $a + B$ with $a \in A$ meets some $f + B$.
steps.detail: If $a \in F$, take $f = a$; the translate meets itself because $B$ is nonempty. If $a \notin F$, maximality says that $F \cup \{a\}$ fails, so $a + B$ meets $f + B$ for some $f \in F$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite a common point to place $a$ in $F + (B - B)$.
steps.detail: A common point gives $a + b = f + b'$ with $b, b' \in B$, so $a = f + (b' - b) \in F + (B - B)$. With step 2, $F$ has both required properties.

concepts.c:finite-set: Finite sets give a maximal family and cardinalities to count.
concepts.c:group: Group translation moves $B$ around and cancels in $a = f + b' - b$.
concepts.c:sumset: The disjoint translates all lie in the sumset $A + B$.
concepts.c:maximal-element: Maximality of $F$ forces every other translate to meet one of $F$.

statement: Let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open [disc](c:ball) $D_R = \{z : |z| < R\}$, with $|f(z)| \le R$ for all $z \in D_R$ and $f(0) = 0$. Then $|f(z)| \le |z|$ for every $z \in D_R$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open disc $D_R$.
The values satisfy $|f(z)| \le R$ for all $z \in D_R$.
The function fixes the centre: $f(0) = 0$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows $f$ to map between any two complex normed spaces, with the open ball of radius $R$ sent into the closed ball of radius $R$.

proofs.name: Quotient and maximum modulus
proofs.slogan: Divide $f$ by $z$, bound the quotient on circles near the boundary, and spread the bound inside by the maximum modulus principle.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma; the point $z = 0$ holds because $f(0) = 0$.

roles.why: Holomorphy makes the quotient $g$ holomorphic, so the maximum modulus principle applies to it.
The bound $|f| \le R$ bounds $g$ by $R/r$ on the circle of radius $r$.
The zero at the centre makes $f(w)/w$ bounded near $0$, so the singularity is removable.

steps.slogan: Divide by $w$ and fill the hole to get a holomorphic $g$ with $f(w) = w\,g(w)$.
steps.detail: Because $f(0) = 0$, the quotient $g(w) = f(w)/w$ tends to $f'(0)$ as $w \to 0$. Riemann's removable singularity theorem extends $g$ to a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on $D_R$.

steps.slogan: Bound $g$ by $R/r$ on each circle $|w| = r$ with $0 < r < R$.
steps.detail: On the circle $|w| = r$ we have $|g(w)| = |f(w)|/r \le R/r$, by the bound on $f$.

steps.slogan: Spread the circle bound inside the closed disc by the maximum modulus principle.
steps.detail: The function $g$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disc $|w| \le r$. Its [maximum modulus](c:maximum-modulus) on that disc is attained on the circle, so $|g(w)| \le R/r$ for $|w| \le r$.

steps.slogan: Let $r$ tend to $R$ and multiply the bound by $|z|$.
steps.detail: Fix $z \in D_R$. Step 3 gives $|g(z)| \le R/r$ for every $r \in (|z|, R)$, so $|g(z)| \le 1$. Hence $|f(z)| = |z|\,|g(z)| \le |z|$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of $f$ and of the quotient $g$ drives the argument.
concepts.c:ball: The disc of radius $R$ is the domain and bounds the values.
concepts.c:maximum-modulus: The maximum modulus of $g$ on a disc sits on its circle.

statement: A channel of [bandwidth](c:bandwidth) $B$ hertz, with average input power at most $S$ and additive white [Gaussian noise](c:gaussian-noise) of power $N$ in the band, has [channel capacity](c:channel-capacity) $C = B\log_2(1 + S/N)$ bits per second.

hypotheses.text: The channel carries [band-limited signals](c:band-limited-signal) with frequencies in $[-B, B]$ hertz.
The noise is additive, white and Gaussian with two-sided spectral density $N_0/2$, so $N = N_0 B$, and independent of the input.
The average input power is at most $S$.

conclusion: The largest rate of reliable transmission is $C = B\log_2(1 + S/N)$ bits per second.

proofs.name: Sampling and the Gaussian channel
proofs.slogan: Sample the band-limited channel into $2B$ uses per second of a discrete Gaussian channel, whose capacity per use is $\tfrac12\log_2(1 + S/N)$ by an entropy bound.
proofs.scope: The theorem under the standard idealization that signals of duration $T$ have $2BT$ degrees of freedom. The prolate spheroidal analysis of Slepian, Landau and Pollak makes that step exact in the limit.

roles.why: Band limitation turns each signal into $2B$ real samples per second.
White Gaussian noise gives independent Gaussian sample noise of variance $N_0/2$, independent of the input.
The power limit bounds the input variance per sample.

steps.slogan: Replace the band-limited signals by $2B$ real samples per second.
steps.detail: By the sampling theorem a signal in the band is fixed by its samples at rate $2B$, in the orthonormal basis of shifted sinc functions. The noise coordinates in this basis are independent $N(0, N_0/2)$ variables.

steps.slogan: Reduce to $2B$ uses per second of a discrete channel $Y = X + Z$.
steps.detail: Each use has input power $P = S/(2B)$, because energy $ST$ spreads over $2BT$ samples, and noise [variance](c:variance) $\sigma^2 = N_0/2 = N/(2B)$. So $P/\sigma^2 = S/N$.

steps.slogan: Express the capacity per use as the largest mutual information under the power limit.
steps.detail: The noisy-channel coding theorem, in its form for power-limited continuous channels, gives the capacity per use as the maximum of the [mutual information](c:mutual-information) $I(X; Y)$ over inputs with $E X^2 \le P$.

steps.slogan: Bound the output entropy by the entropy of a Gaussian with the same variance.
steps.detail: Since $Z$ is independent of $X$, $I(X; Y) = h(Y) - h(Z)$ with $\operatorname{Var} Y \le P + \sigma^2$. The [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) maximizes differential entropy at fixed variance, so $I \le \tfrac12\log_2(1 + P/\sigma^2)$, with equality for $X \sim N(0, P)$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the capacity per sample by $2B$ samples per second.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give $\tfrac12\log_2(1 + S/N)$ bits per sample. Hence $C = 2B \cdot \tfrac12\log_2(1 + S/N) = B\log_2(1 + S/N)$ bits per second.

concepts.c:bandwidth: The bandwidth fixes the number of samples per second.
concepts.c:gaussian-noise: Gaussian noise makes the channel an additive Gaussian channel per sample.
concepts.c:channel-capacity: Capacity is the maximal mutual information times the sample rate.
concepts.c:band-limited-signal: Band-limited signals are determined by their samples at rate $2B$.
concepts.c:variance: The variances of signal and noise set the signal-to-noise ratio.
concepts.c:mutual-information: Capacity per use is the largest mutual information under the power limit.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: The Gaussian input maximizes output entropy and attains the bound.

source.note: Shannon's derivation (C. E. Shannon, Communication in the presence of noise, Proceedings of the IRE 37, 1949), as in Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, chapter 9 (Gaussian channel, band-limited channels).

statement: For a short [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $0 \to M \xrightarrow{f} N \xrightarrow{g} P \to 0$ of [modules](c:module), these are equivalent: (a) $g s = \mathrm{id}_P$ for a [module homomorphism](c:module-homomorphism) $s$; (b) $r f = \mathrm{id}_M$ for some $r$; (c) an isomorphism $e\colon N \to M \oplus P$ onto the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) turns $f$ into the inclusion and $g$ into the projection.

hypotheses.text: The sequence is exact at $N$: $\operatorname{im} f = \ker g$.
The map $f$ is injective.
The map $g$ is surjective.

conclusion: A section of $g$, a retraction of $f$ and a compatible splitting $N \cong M \oplus P$ exist together or not at all: the sequence is then a [split exact sequence](c:split-exact-sequence).

formal.difference: The declaration takes modules over a semiring whose underlying additive groups are commutative groups, and states (c) as $f = e^{-1} \circ \mathrm{inl}$ and $g = \mathrm{snd} \circ e$.

proofs.name: Explicit isomorphisms
proofs.slogan: Build the splitting isomorphism from a section or from a retraction, and read a section and a retraction off a splitting.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma: (a) and (c) are equivalent, and (b) and (c) are equivalent.

roles.why: Exactness writes every element of $\ker g$ as $f(m)$, which gives surjectivity and injectivity of the two maps.
Injectivity of $f$ makes the map $(m, p) \mapsto f(m) + s(p)$ injective.
Surjectivity of $g$ makes the map $n \mapsto (r(n), g(n))$ surjective.

steps.slogan: Build the isomorphism $(m, p) \mapsto f(m) + s(p)$ from a section $s$.
steps.detail: Applying $g$ to $f(m) + s(p) = 0$ gives $p = 0$, then $f(m) = 0$ gives $m = 0$. For $n \in N$, $n - s(g(n)) \in \ker g = \operatorname{im} f$, so the map is onto; its inverse $e$ sends $f$ to the inclusion and $g$ to the projection.

steps.slogan: Recover a section $s = e^{-1} \circ \mathrm{inr}$ from a splitting $e$.
steps.detail: For $p \in P$, $g(e^{-1}(0, p))$ is the $P$-coordinate of $(0, p)$, which is $p$. So $g s = \mathrm{id}_P$.

steps.slogan: Build the isomorphism $n \mapsto (r(n), g(n))$ from a retraction $r$.
steps.detail: If $g(n) = 0$, then $n = f(m)$ and $r(n) = m$, so $r(n) = 0$ forces $n = 0$. Given $(m, p)$, choose $n_0$ with $g(n_0) = p$; then $n = n_0 - f(r(n_0)) + f(m)$ maps to $(m, p)$. The map sends $f(m)$ to $(m, 0)$.

steps.slogan: Recover a retraction $r = \mathrm{fst} \circ e$ from a splitting $e$.
steps.detail: For $m \in M$, $e(f(m)) = (m, 0)$, whose first coordinate is $m$. So $r f = \mathrm{id}_M$, and $r$ is a [module homomorphism](c:module-homomorphism).

steps.slogan: Chain the four implications into the equivalence of the three conditions.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give (a) if and only if (c). Steps 3 and 4 give (b) if and only if (c). Hence (a), (b) and (c) are equivalent.

concepts.c:exact-sequence: Exactness identifies $\ker g$ with the image of $f$.
concepts.c:module: All maps are module maps, so the sums and projections stay linear.
concepts.c:module-homomorphism: Sections and retractions must be module homomorphisms, not just maps.
concepts.c:direct-sum: The splitting identifies $N$ with the direct sum $M \oplus P$.
concepts.c:split-exact-sequence: The three conditions are the equivalent forms of being split.

statement: Let $U$ and $V$ be strongly continuous [unitary representations](c:unitary-representation) of $\mathbb{R}^n$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ with the [Weyl relations](c:weyl-relation) $U(a)V(b) = e^{i a\cdot b}V(b)U(a)$ and no common closed invariant subspace except $0$ and $H$. Then a unitary $T\colon H \to L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ carries $U(a)$ to $\psi(x) \mapsto \psi(x + a)$ and $V(b)$ to $\psi(x) \mapsto e^{i b\cdot x}\psi(x)$.

hypotheses.text: The maps $U$ and $V$ are strongly continuous [unitary representations](c:unitary-representation) of $\mathbb{R}^n$ on $H$.
They satisfy the [Weyl relations](c:weyl-relation) $U(a)V(b) = e^{i a\cdot b}V(b)U(a)$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^n$.
The pair is [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation): only $0$ and $H$ are closed subspaces invariant under all $U(a)$ and $V(b)$.

conclusion: The pair $(U, V)$ is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger pair on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$; equivalently the [Heisenberg group](c:heisenberg-group) has one irreducible unitary representation with this central character.

proofs.name: Gaussian projection
proofs.slogan: Average the Weyl operators against a Gaussian to get a projection whose range vectors generate mutually orthogonal copies of one model representation.
proofs.scope: An outline of von Neumann's proof; the operator identities for the Gaussian average rest on the cited work. Without irreducibility the same steps write $H$ as an orthogonal sum of copies of the Schrödinger representation.

roles.why: Unitarity and strong continuity make the Weyl operators unitary and their Gaussian average a bounded operator.
The Weyl relations give the twisted product law that the Gaussian identities need.
Irreducibility leaves a single cyclic summand.

steps.slogan: Combine $U$ and $V$ into Weyl operators $W(a, b) = e^{-i a\cdot b/2}U(a)V(b)$.
steps.detail: The Weyl relations give $W(z)W(z') = e^{i\sigma(z, z')/2}W(z + z')$ for the standard symplectic form $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, and $W(z)^* = W(-z)$. They are the exponentiated [canonical commutation relations](c:canonical-commutation-relation).

steps.slogan: Average $W$ against a Gaussian to get a nonzero [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) $P$.
steps.detail: Set $P = (2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{-|z|^2/4}W(z)\,dz$. Gaussian integrals give $P^* = P$ and $P W(z) P = e^{-|z|^2/4}P$, so $P^2 = P$. If $P = 0$, then $W(z)^* P W(z) = 0$ for all $z$, and a Fourier argument gives $\langle \varphi, \psi\rangle = 0$ for all vectors, which is false.

steps.slogan: Compute the inner products of the vectors $W(z)\varphi$ for $\varphi$ in the range of $P$.
steps.detail: For $\varphi, \psi \in \operatorname{ran} P$, step 2 gives $\langle W(z)\varphi, W(z')\psi\rangle = c\,e^{-|z - z'|^2/4}\langle\varphi, \psi\rangle$ with a factor $|c| = 1$ that depends only on $z, z'$. So orthogonal $\varphi, \psi$ generate orthogonal cyclic subspaces, and unit $\varphi, \psi$ generate unitarily equivalent ones.

steps.slogan: Show that the cyclic subspaces of an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran} P$ fill $H$.
steps.detail: The orthogonal complement $K$ of their sum is invariant under all $W(z)$. If $K \ne 0$, step 2 applied to $K$ gives a nonzero vector of $\operatorname{ran} P$ inside $K$, which is impossible.

steps.slogan: Use irreducibility and the Schrödinger model to identify the single summand.
steps.detail: Irreducibility leaves one cyclic subspace, so $H$ is generated by one unit vector of $\operatorname{ran} P$. The Schrödinger pair satisfies the hypotheses and is irreducible, so step 3 gives a unitary $T$ onto $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ that intertwines the two pairs.

concepts.c:unitary-representation: Both one-parameter families act by unitary operators.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: The orthogonal decomposition into cyclic subspaces needs a Hilbert space.
concepts.c:weyl-relation: The Weyl relations fix the product law of the Weyl operators.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducibility leaves only one cyclic summand.
concepts.c:heisenberg-group: The pair is a representation of the Heisenberg group.
concepts.c:canonical-commutation-relation: The Weyl relations exponentiate the canonical commutation relations.
concepts.c:orthogonal-projection: The Gaussian average is a projection that picks the vacuum vectors.

source.ref: J. von Neumann, Die Eindeutigkeit der Schrödingerschen Operatoren, Mathematische Annalen 104 (1931), 570-578
source.note: von Neumann's Gaussian projection proof; G. B. Folland, Harmonic Analysis in Phase Space (Princeton, 1989), chapter 1, gives a modern account.

statement: Every [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-group) [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $G$ is isomorphic to a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $\mathbb{Z}^r \oplus \mathbb{Z}/p_1^{e_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathbb{Z}/p_k^{e_k}$ of [cyclic groups](c:cyclic-group), with primes $p_i$ and exponents $e_i \ge 1$. The rank $r$ and the list of [prime powers](c:prime-power) $p_i^{e_i}$, up to order, are determined by $G$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group).
The group $G$ is [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-group).

conclusion: $G \cong \mathbb{Z}^r \oplus \bigoplus_i \mathbb{Z}/p_i^{e_i}$, with $r$ and the multiset of prime powers unique.

formal.difference: The declaration gives existence only, with $\mathbb{Z}^r$ written as finitely supported functions on $\mathrm{Fin}\, n$; it does not state the uniqueness of $r$ and of the prime powers.

proofs.name: Free part, torsion part and primary parts
proofs.slogan: Split off a free quotient, decompose the finite torsion subgroup into primary parts, and break each primary part into cyclic groups.
proofs.scope: Existence and uniqueness; the trivial group is the case $r = k = 0$. The uniqueness step goes beyond the declaration.

roles.why: Commutativity makes $G$ a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, so the [torsion subgroup](c:torsion-subgroup) and the primary parts are subgroups.
Finite generation makes $G/T$ free of finite rank and $T$ finite.

steps.slogan: Show that $G/T$ is a free abelian group of finite rank, for the torsion subgroup $T$.
steps.detail: The quotient $H = G/T$ is finitely generated and torsion-free. For a maximal independent subset $x_1, \dots, x_r$ of its generators, some $d \ge 1$ has $dH \subseteq \langle x_1, \dots, x_r\rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}^r$; so $H \cong dH$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}^r$, which is free by induction on $r$.

steps.slogan: Lift a basis of $G/T$ to split $G \cong T \oplus \mathbb{Z}^r$.
steps.detail: Sending a basis of the [free abelian group](c:free-abelian-group) $G/T$ to chosen preimages defines a section of $G \to G/T$. The splitting lemma gives $G \cong T \oplus G/T$. Then $T$ is a quotient of $G$, so finitely generated and torsion, hence finite.

steps.slogan: Decompose the finite group $T$ into its $p$-primary parts $T_p$.
steps.detail: If $|T| = \prod_p p^{a_p}$, let $T_p = \{x : p^{a_p}x = 0\}$. Bezout identities for the coprime factors of $|T|$ give $T = \bigoplus_p T_p$, as in the Chinese remainder theorem.

steps.slogan: Split each $T_p$ into cyclic $p$-groups by removing an element of maximal order.
steps.detail: Let $x \in T_p$ have maximal order $p^e$. By induction on $|T_p|$, $T_p/\langle x\rangle$ is a sum of cyclic groups, and their generators lift to elements of the same orders because $p^e T_p = 0$. The lifts and $x$ split $T_p$ into cyclic groups of prime power order.

steps.slogan: Read off the rank and the prime powers from invariants of $G$.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be the [torsion subgroup](c:torsion-subgroup) and $T_p$ its $p$-power part; then $G/T \cong \mathbb{Z}^r$, and $|(G/T)/2(G/T)| = 2^r$ fixes $r$. The number of summands $\mathbb{Z}/p^e$ with $e \ge j$ equals $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p} p^{j-1}T_p/p^jT_p$, which depends only on $G$; this gives uniqueness.

concepts.c:finitely-generated-group: Finite generation makes the free part finite rank and the torsion finite.
concepts.c:abelian-group: An abelian group is a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, so module arguments apply.
concepts.c:direct-sum: The proof builds the decomposition one direct summand at a time.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: The final summands are cyclic groups.
concepts.c:prime-power: The torsion summands have prime power order.
concepts.c:torsion-subgroup: The torsion subgroup is the finite part split off first.
concepts.c:free-abelian-group: A free quotient lifts, so the extension splits.

source.note: mathlib applies Module.equiv_free_prod_directSum, the structure theorem over the principal ideal domain of integers (via Module.Finite.iff_addGroup_fg), and identifies each quotient by a prime power with ZMod (Int.quotientSpanEquivZMod); the steps follow that theorem's free-part and torsion-part route.

proofs.name: Smith normal form of the relations
proofs.slogan: Present the group by integer relations, diagonalize the relation matrix by row and column operations, and split the cyclic factors by the Chinese remainder theorem.
proofs.scope: Existence and uniqueness; the uniqueness step is the same invariant count as in the first proof.

roles.why: An abelian group with $m$ generators is a quotient of $\mathbb{Z}^m$.
Finitely many generators give a finite presentation matrix.

steps.slogan: Present $G$ as $\mathbb{Z}^m/K$ with $K$ spanned by the columns of an integer matrix $A$.
steps.detail: Generators $g_1, \dots, g_m$ give a surjection $\mathbb{Z}^m \to G$ with kernel $K$. Subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}^m$ are generated by at most $m$ elements, so $K$ is the column span of an integer matrix $A$.

steps.slogan: Reduce $A$ to [Smith normal form](c:smith-normal-form) by invertible integer row and column operations.
steps.detail: Repeated division with remainder on the entries gives invertible $P, Q$ with $PAQ = \operatorname{diag}(d_1, \dots, d_s, 0, \dots)$ and $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \cdots \mid d_s$, $d_i \ge 1$. Row operations change the basis of $\mathbb{Z}^m$; column operations change the generators of $K$.

steps.slogan: Read off $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/d_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathbb{Z}/d_s \oplus \mathbb{Z}^{m-s}$ from the diagonal form.
steps.detail: In the new basis $e_1, \dots, e_m$ of $\mathbb{Z}^m$, $K = d_1\mathbb{Z}e_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus d_s\mathbb{Z}e_s$. So the quotient is the stated [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of [cyclic groups](c:cyclic-group), with $r = m - s$.

steps.slogan: Split each $\mathbb{Z}/d_i$ into prime power factors by the Chinese remainder theorem.
steps.detail: If $d = \prod_p p^{a_p}$, the Chinese remainder theorem gives $\mathbb{Z}/d \cong \bigoplus_p \mathbb{Z}/p^{a_p}$, because the [prime powers](c:prime-power) are pairwise coprime.

steps.slogan: Read off the rank and the prime powers from invariants of $G$.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be the [torsion subgroup](c:torsion-subgroup) and $T_p$ its $p$-power part; then $G/T \cong \mathbb{Z}^r$, and $|(G/T)/2(G/T)| = 2^r$ fixes $r$. The number of summands $\mathbb{Z}/p^e$ with $e \ge j$ equals $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p} p^{j-1}T_p/p^jT_p$, which depends only on $G$; this gives uniqueness.

concepts.c:finitely-generated-group: Finitely many generators give a finite relation matrix.
concepts.c:abelian-group: Commutativity makes the group a quotient of $\mathbb{Z}^m$.
concepts.c:direct-sum: The diagonal form splits the quotient into a direct sum.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: Each diagonal entry gives one cyclic summand.
concepts.c:prime-power: The Chinese remainder theorem splits cyclic groups into prime power parts.
concepts.c:smith-normal-form: The diagonal relation matrix exhibits the cyclic decomposition.
concepts.c:torsion-subgroup: The torsion subgroup and its primary parts carry the uniqueness invariants.

source.note: The Smith normal form proof, as in Jacobson, Basic Algebra I, chapter 3 (modules over a principal ideal domain).

statement: For all natural numbers $n$ and $p$, $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^p = \frac{1}{p+1}\sum_{i=0}^{p} \binom{p+1}{i} B_i\, n^{p+1-i}$, where the $B_i$ are the [Bernoulli numbers](c:bernoulli-number) with $B_1 = -1/2$ and the $\binom{p+1}{i}$ are [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient).
conclusion: The power sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^p$ is a polynomial in $n$ of degree $p + 1$ with the stated Bernoulli coefficients.

proofs.name: Exponential generating functions
proofs.slogan: Sum the exponentials $e^{kt}$ as a geometric series, multiply by the Bernoulli series $t/(e^t - 1)$, and compare the coefficients of $t^{p+1}$.
proofs.scope: All $n, p \ge 0$ with $0^0 = 1$; for $n = 0$ both sides are $0$. The computation takes place in the ring of formal power series over $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps.slogan: Write the Bernoulli numbers as the coefficients of the series $t/(e^t - 1)$.
steps.detail: The recursion $\sum_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m+1}{i}B_i = 0$ for $m \ge 1$, with $B_0 = 1$, says that $\big(\sum_i B_i t^i/i!\big)(e^t - 1) = t$ in the [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) ring: the coefficient of $t^{m+1}$ is $\sum_i \binom{m+1}{i}B_i/(m+1)!$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the geometric sum $\sum_{k<n} e^{kt}$ by the factor $e^t - 1$.
steps.detail: The product telescopes: $(e^t - 1)\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} e^{kt} = e^{nt} - 1$. This is the finite geometric series with ratio $e^t$, an identity of power series.

steps.slogan: Cancel $e^t - 1$ to get $t\sum_{k<n} e^{kt} = \frac{t}{e^t - 1}(e^{nt} - 1)$.
steps.detail: By steps 1 and 2, both sides become $t(e^{nt} - 1)$ after multiplication by $e^t - 1$. The power series ring over $\mathbb{Q}$ has no zero divisors and $e^t - 1 \ne 0$, so the two sides are equal.

steps.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $t^{p+1}$ on the two sides.
steps.detail: On the left the coefficient is $\sum_k k^p/p!$. On the right the Cauchy product with $e^{nt} - 1 = \sum_{j \ge 1} n^j t^j/j!$ gives $\sum_{i=0}^{p} B_i n^{p+1-i}/(i!\,(p+1-i)!)$; multiply by $p!$ and use $\frac{p!}{i!(p+1-i)!} = \frac{1}{p+1}\binom{p+1}{i}$.

concepts.c:bernoulli-number: The Bernoulli numbers are the coefficients of $t/(e^t - 1)$.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: Binomial coefficients appear when factorials from the Cauchy product combine.
concepts.c:formal-power-series: The identities are equalities of formal power series over $\mathbb{Q}$.

source.note: mathlib multiplies the geometric sum of powers of exp (geom_sum_mul) by bernoulliPowerSeries via bernoulliPowerSeries_mul_exp_sub_one, cancels exp minus 1 with mul_right_inj', and reads coefficients with PowerSeries.coeff_mul.

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) and $W$ a [submanifold](c:submanifold) of the [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle) $J^k(X, Y)$. Then the smooth maps $f\colon X \to Y$ whose $k$-jet extension $j^k f$ is [transverse](c:transversality) to $W$ form a residual set, a countable intersection of open [dense](c:dense-set) sets, in $C^\infty(X, Y)$ with the [Whitney topology](c:c-infinity-topology); in particular they are dense.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X$ and $Y$ are [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold), Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary.
The set $W$ is a smooth [submanifold](c:submanifold) of $J^k(X, Y)$.

conclusion: The set $\{f : j^k f \pitchfork W\}$ is residual, hence dense, in $C^\infty(X, Y)$ with the Whitney $C^\infty$ topology.

proofs.name: Parametric transversality and Baire
proofs.slogan: Show by Sard's theorem that small polynomial perturbations make the jet transverse on each compact piece of $W$, then intersect countably many open dense sets.
proofs.scope: An outline: the openness of each set $T_r$ and the Baire property of $C^\infty(X, Y)$ rest on the cited text.

roles.why: Second countability gives countably many charts, and $C^\infty(X, Y)$ is a [Baire space](c:baire-space).
The preimage of the submanifold $W$ under a transverse family is a manifold, which Sard's theorem needs.

steps.slogan: Prove that a transverse family of maps has transverse members for almost every parameter.
steps.detail: If $F\colon X \times S \to Z$ is transverse to $W$, then $F^{-1}(W)$ is a manifold, and $F_s \pitchfork W$ exactly when $s$ is a [regular value](c:regular-value) of the projection $F^{-1}(W) \to S$. Sard's theorem makes almost every $s$ regular.

steps.slogan: Cover $W$ by countably many compact pieces $W_r$ inside jet coordinate charts.
steps.detail: Second countability gives compact sets $W_r$ with $\bigcup_r W_r = W$, each in a chart of $J^k(X, Y)$ over a chart of $X$. Let $T_r$ be the set of $f$ with $j^k f$ transverse to $W$ at the points of $W_r$; the transverse maps form $\bigcap_r T_r$.

steps.slogan: Show that each set $T_r$ is open in the Whitney topology.
steps.detail: Transversality at the points of the compact set $W_r$ is a condition on finitely many derivatives of $f$ over a compact set. It survives small perturbations in the Whitney $C^\infty$ topology, as the cited text proves.

steps.slogan: Perturb $f$ by small polynomial terms to make $j^k f$ transverse on $W_r$.
steps.detail: In local coordinates set $f_s(x) = f(x) + \rho(x)\sum_{|\alpha| \le k} s_\alpha x^\alpha$ with a bump function $\rho$. The map $(x, s) \mapsto j^k f_s(x)$ is a submersion onto the jet fibres near the chart, so step 1 gives arbitrarily small $s$ with $f_s \in T_r$.

steps.slogan: Intersect the countably many open dense sets $T_r$ in the Baire space $C^\infty(X, Y)$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 make each $T_r$ open and dense, so $\bigcap_r T_r$ is residual. The space $C^\infty(X, Y)$ with the Whitney $C^\infty$ topology is a [Baire space](c:baire-space), so this residual set is dense.

concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Charts of the manifolds localize the problem to coordinates.
concepts.c:submanifold: Transversality is measured against the submanifold $W$ of jet space.
concepts.c:jet-bundle: The jet extension $j^k f$ is a map into the jet bundle.
concepts.c:transversality: Transversality of $j^k f$ to $W$ is the generic property proved.
concepts.c:dense-set: Each perturbation step shows that $T_r$ is dense.
concepts.c:c-infinity-topology: Openness, density and the Baire property refer to this topology.
concepts.c:baire-space: A countable intersection of open dense sets is dense in a Baire space.
concepts.c:regular-value: Sard's theorem supplies regular values of the parameter projection.

source.ref: M. Golubitsky and V. Guillemin, Stable Mappings and Their Singularities, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 14, Springer, 1973
source.note: Chapter II, section 4 proves the theorem through the parametric transversality lemma and Sard's theorem, and chapter II, section 3 proves that the Whitney topology is Baire.

statement: Let $X$ be a closed embedded [submanifold](c:submanifold) of a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$. Then some open neighborhood $U$ of $X$ in $M$ is [diffeomorphic](c:diffeomorph) to the total space of the [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle) $NX$, by a diffeomorphism that sends the [zero section](c:zero-section) to $X$ by the identity.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold), Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary.
The set $X$ is a closed embedded [submanifold](c:submanifold) of $M$ without boundary.

conclusion: There is a diffeomorphism $NX \to U$ onto an open neighborhood $U$ of $X$ that is the identity on the zero section.

proofs.name: Normal exponential map
proofs.slogan: Send normal vectors into $M$ by the exponential map, make it injective near the zero section, and stretch that neighborhood onto the whole bundle.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $X = M$ the normal bundle has rank $0$ and $U = M$. The argument uses that $X$ is embedded, not that it is closed.

roles.why: A second countable Hausdorff manifold carries a Riemannian metric, built with a partition of unity.
An embedded submanifold has a smooth normal bundle, and its subspace topology lets the sequence argument conclude injectivity.

steps.slogan: Choose a Riemannian metric and realize $NX$ as the orthogonal complement of $TX$.
steps.detail: A partition of unity glues local inner products into a metric on $M$. Then $N_xX \cong (T_xX)^\perp \subseteq T_xM$, and these spaces form a smooth vector bundle over $X$.

steps.slogan: Define $E(x, v) = \exp_x(v)$ on a neighborhood of the zero section of $NX$.
steps.detail: The Riemannian [exponential map](c:exponential-map) is smooth on an open subset of $TM$ that contains the zero section. Its restriction to $NX$ is the smooth map $E$, with $E(x, 0) = x$.

steps.slogan: Show that $E$ is a local diffeomorphism near each point of the zero section.
steps.detail: At $(x, 0)$ the tangent space of $NX$ is $T_xX \oplus N_xX$, and $dE$ is the identity onto $T_xM = T_xX \oplus N_xX$. The inverse function theorem makes $E$ a [local diffeomorphism](c:local-diffeomorphism) near $(x, 0)$.

steps.slogan: Shrink to a neighborhood $\{|v| < \delta(x)\}$ on which $E$ is injective.
steps.detail: Over each compact piece of an exhaustion of $X$, a sequence argument gives a radius below which $E$ is injective, because $E$ is injective on the zero section. Patching these radii gives a smooth $\delta > 0$; then $E$ is an injective local diffeomorphism on $V_\delta$, hence a diffeomorphism onto an open $U$.

steps.slogan: Stretch the fibres to carry all of $NX$ onto the neighborhood $V_\delta$.
steps.detail: The map $(x, v) \mapsto (x, \delta(x)\,v/\sqrt{1 + |v|^2})$ is a diffeomorphism of $NX$ onto $V_\delta$ that fixes the zero section. Composed with $E$, it gives the required diffeomorphism $NX \to U$.

concepts.c:submanifold: The submanifold is the zero section of its tubular neighborhood.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The ambient manifold carries the metric and the exponential map.
concepts.c:diffeomorph: The result is a diffeomorphism from the bundle onto a neighborhood.
concepts.c:normal-bundle: Normal vectors parametrize the points near $X$.
concepts.c:zero-section: The diffeomorphism is the identity on the zero section.
concepts.c:exponential-map: Geodesics in normal directions sweep out the neighborhood.
concepts.c:local-diffeomorphism: The inverse function theorem makes $E$ a local diffeomorphism there.

source.note: The normal exponential map proof, as in J. M. Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds (2nd ed., 2018), chapter 5, with the fibre stretching of M. W. Hirsch, Differential Topology, chapter 4.

statement: A finite [graph](c:graph) $G$ has a [perfect matching](c:perfect-matching) if and only if, for every set $U$ of vertices, the graph $G - U$ has at most $|U|$ [odd components](c:odd-component).

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is a finite simple [graph](c:graph).

conclusion: $G$ has a perfect matching exactly when no vertex set $U$ leaves more than $|U|$ odd components in $G - U$.

proofs.name: Edge-maximal graph without a perfect matching
proofs.slogan: Count matched partners for necessity; for sufficiency, add edges until any further edge creates a perfect matching and show that the universal vertices violate the condition.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching, and an odd number of vertices is handled by $U = \emptyset$.

roles.why: Finiteness gives parity counts and an edge-maximal supergraph after finitely many added edges.

steps.slogan: Match each odd component of $G - U$ to a distinct vertex of $U$.
steps.detail: In a perfect matching, an odd component $C$ cannot be matched inside itself, so some vertex of $C$ is matched to a vertex outside $C$, which lies in $U$. Distinct components get distinct partners, so there are at most $|U|$ odd components.

steps.slogan: Take $U = \emptyset$ when the number of vertices is odd.
steps.detail: If $|V|$ is odd, then $G$ has an odd component and no perfect matching, so $U = \emptyset$ violates the condition. Hence it suffices to treat $|V|$ even with no perfect matching.

steps.slogan: Add edges to get an edge-maximal graph $G^*$ without a perfect matching.

statement: Let $\mu$ be a [finite measure](c:finite-measure). A set $K \subseteq L^1(\mu)$ of [integrable functions](c:l1-space) is relatively [weakly compact](c:weak-compactness) if and only if it is [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability): $\lim_{M \to \infty}\sup_{f \in K}\int_{\{|f| > M\}}|f|\,d\mu = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The measure $\mu$ is a [finite measure](c:finite-measure) on a measurable space $(\Omega, \Sigma)$.
The set $K$ is a subset of [$L^1(\mu)$](c:l1-space).

conclusion: $K$ has weakly compact closure in $L^1(\mu)$ exactly when it is uniformly integrable (Dunford-Pettis theorem).

proofs.name: Weak-star limits and setwise convergence
proofs.slogan: Show that weak-star limits of a uniformly integrable set are integrable densities by Radon-Nikodym, and get the converse from Eberlein-Šmulian and Vitali-Hahn-Saks.
proofs.scope: Both directions, for real or complex $L^1(\mu)$. Uniform integrability is first rewritten as boundedness plus uniform absolute continuity, which uses that $\mu$ is finite.

roles.why: Finiteness of $\mu$ makes uniform integrability equal to boundedness plus uniform absolute continuity, and gives $(L^1)^* = L^\infty$.
Functions of $L^1$ pair with $L^\infty$ and define measures $A \mapsto \int_A f\,d\mu$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite uniform integrability as boundedness plus uniform absolute continuity.
steps.detail: The bound $\int_A|f| \le M\mu(A) + \int_{\{|f| > M\}}|f|$ gives one direction, and $\mu(|f| > M) \le \|f\|_1/M$ gives the other. So $K$ is uniformly integrable exactly when it is bounded and, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, some $\delta > 0$ gives $\int_A|f| < \varepsilon$ for all $f \in K$ when $\mu(A) < \delta$.

steps.slogan: Embed $L^1(\mu)$ in the dual of $L^\infty(\mu)$ and take the weak-star closure of $K$.
steps.detail: Each $f \in L^1$ acts on $L^\infty$ by integration, and the weak topology of $L^1$ is the restriction of the [weak-* topology](c:weak-topology-2) because $(L^1)^* = L^\infty$. A bounded $K$ has a weak-star compact closure $\overline{K}$ in the [dual space](c:dual-space) by the Banach-Alaoglu theorem.

steps.slogan: Show that every point of the weak-star closure is an integrable density.
steps.detail:
For $\varphi \in \overline{K}$, the set function $
u(A) = \varphi(1_A)$ keeps the bound $|
u(A)| \le \varepsilon$ when $\mu(A) < \delta$, so it is countably additive and [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure). Radon-Nikodym gives $g \in L^1$ with $
u(A) = \int_A g$, and $\varphi = g$ on the dense simple functions, hence on $L^\infty$.

steps.slogan: Extract a weakly convergent sequence from a weakly compact set that is not uniformly integrable.
steps.detail: A relatively weakly compact $K$ is bounded. If it is not uniformly absolutely continuous, there are $\varepsilon > 0$, $f_n \in K$ and sets $A_n$ with $\mu(A_n) < 2^{-n}$ and $|\int_{A_n} f_n| \ge \varepsilon$, after shrinking $A_n$ to a set where one part of $f_n$ has fixed sign. Eberlein-Šmulian gives a weakly convergent subsequence.

steps.slogan: Apply the Vitali-Hahn-Saks theorem to the measures $A \mapsto \int_A f_n\,d\mu$.
steps.detail: Weak convergence, tested on $1_A \in L^\infty$, makes $\int_A f_n$ converge for every measurable $A$. Vitali-Hahn-Saks then makes these measures uniformly absolutely continuous, which contradicts $|\int_{A_n} f_n| \ge \varepsilon$ with $\mu(A_n) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 put the weak-star closure of a uniformly integrable $K$ inside $L^1$, where it is weakly compact. Steps 4 and 5, with step 1, show that a relatively weakly compact set is uniformly integrable.

concepts.c:finite-measure: Finiteness lets uniform integrability split into boundedness and absolute continuity.
concepts.c:l1-space: The theorem describes the weakly compact subsets of $L^1(\mu)$.
concepts.c:weak-compactness: Relative weak compactness is the property characterized.
concepts.c:uniform-integrability: Uniform integrability is the measure-theoretic side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:weak-topology-2: Weak-star compactness in the dual of $L^\infty$ supplies limit points.
concepts.c:dual-space: The set $K$ sits inside the dual of $L^\infty$.
concepts.c:absolutely-continuous-measure: Absolute continuity of the limit set function allows Radon-Nikodym.

Dunford and B. J. Pettis, Linear operations on summable functions, Trans. AMS 47 (1940), 323-392.

statement: Every [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) is [biholomorphic](c:biholomorphic-function) to exactly one of the [unit disc](c:unit-disc), the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ and the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface), a connected complex manifold of dimension one.
The surface $X$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space).

conclusion: $X$ is biholomorphic to the disc, the plane or the sphere, and to only one of them.

proofs.name: Riemann-Roch and Green's functions
proofs.slogan: Map a compact surface to the sphere by Riemann-Roch, map a noncompact surface onto the disc or the plane by Green's functions on an exhaustion, and separate the models.
proofs.scope: An outline of the proof in the cited text; the potential theory, the exhaustion and the limit rest on it. The compact and noncompact cases are treated separately.

roles.why: The complex structure gives meromorphic functions, harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem on $X$.
Simple connectivity gives genus $0$ and global harmonic conjugates, so the maps are single-valued.

steps.slogan: Map a compact simply connected surface onto the sphere by a function with one simple pole.
steps.detail: Simple connectivity forces genus $0$. Riemann-Roch then gives a meromorphic function with a single simple pole; it has degree one, so it is a biholomorphism onto the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere).

steps.slogan: Map each simply connected regular domain onto the disc through its Green's function.
steps.detail: On a relatively compact regular domain $Y$ of a noncompact $X$, Perron's method solves the Dirichlet problem and gives a Green's function $G(\cdot, a)$ with a logarithmic pole at $a$. On simply connected $Y$, $G$ has a harmonic conjugate $G^*$, and $f = e^{-(G + iG^*)}$ maps $Y$ biholomorphically onto the [unit disc](c:unit-disc).

steps.slogan: Exhaust the noncompact surface by increasing simply connected regular domains and normalize their maps.
steps.detail: The cited text writes $X = \bigcup_n Y_n$ with regular domains $Y_n \Subset Y_{n+1}$, each simply connected because $X$ is. Rescaled maps $f_n\colon Y_n \to \{|w| < r_n\}$ with $f_n(a) = 0$ and derivative $1$ in a fixed chart have increasing radii $r_n$ by the Schwarz lemma.

steps.slogan: Pass to a locally uniform limit of the normalized maps by normal families.
steps.detail: The maps $f_n$ form a normal family on each $Y_m$, and a diagonal subsequence converges locally uniformly; Hurwitz's theorem keeps the limit injective. The limit maps $X$ onto the disc of radius $\lim r_n$ when this limit is finite, and onto $\mathbb{C}$ when it is infinite.

steps.slogan: Separate the three models by compactness and by Liouville's theorem.
steps.detail: The sphere is compact and the other two are not. A biholomorphism from $\mathbb{C}$ onto the disc would be a bounded nonconstant entire function, which Liouville's theorem excludes; so each $X$ has exactly one model.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity makes harmonic conjugates and the mapping functions single-valued.
concepts.c:riemann-surface: The theorem classifies simply connected Riemann surfaces.
concepts.c:biholomorphic-function: The classification is up to biholomorphic maps.
concepts.c:unit-disc: The disc is the model reached through Green's functions.
concepts.c:riemann-sphere: The sphere is the model for compact surfaces.

source.ref: O. Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 81, Springer, 1981, section 27 (The Riemann mapping theorem)
source.note: Forster proves the theorem by Riemann-Roch in the compact case and by Green's functions on an exhaustion of the noncompact surface; the theorem is due to Koebe and Poincare (1907).
